The panel presents two rows of small rectangular windows that illuminate as either yellow, red, or green. Also included with this group, but located on the center instrument panel, are three caution/warning lights associated with the TAWS.

items.lede: Flights through icing conditions should be avoided if possible. However, if flight in these conditions is necessary, make use of anti-icing and deicing systems to prevent the formation of ice on the pitot tubes, lift detector, fuel vents, engine air intake, and propeller blades. Deicer boots are provided to remove ice from the wing and tail leading edges.

The EFIS is made up of a pilot side and copilot side system. Each side is functionally and physically isolated from each other, and is capable of functioning as a complete, independent system.

items.lede: "FPWANTS" is a memory aid for the typical tasks to be accomplished before an IFR flight. Physically going to Base Ops may not be required considering the capability to accomplish the appropriate tasks via computer, fax, or telephone.

items.title: Brake fire
items.lede: If an emergency situation dictates immediate discontinuation of engine operation such as fire, fire warning light, brake fire, flameout on deck, etc., request assistance as necessary and perform the Emergency Shutdown on Deck checklist.

items.title: Brake system malfunctions
items.lede: No emergency brake system is provided. Reverse or beta (zero thrust) should be used to taxi and to slow the aircraft after landing.

items.title: Brake system
items.lede: The main landing wheels are equipped with hydraulic brakes actuated by master cylinders attached to each of the rudder pedals for both pilot and copilot brakes. No emergency brake system is provided.

items.title: Canned routes
items.lede: A stereo route is a routinely used route of flight established by users and ARTCC identified by a coded name. These routes simplify flight plan handling and communications.

items.title: Continuous descent final approach (CDFA)
items.lede: Continuous Descent Final Approach (CDFA) is a technique for flying the final approach segment of a non-precision approach as a continuous descent. The technique is consistent with stabilized approach procedures and has no level off. A CDFA starts from an altitude/height at or above the FAF and proceeds to an altitude/height 50 ft above the MDA.

items.title: Center instrument panel
items.lede: Engine instruments are all located in the left center section of the instrument panel. The RTU provides tuning and mode selection capability for the connected CNI equipment and is mounted on the center instrument panel.

items.title: Combat cruise checkpoints
items.lede: Combat formations are designed to provide maximum flight flexibility and individual aircraft freedom to enhance maneuverability, lookout doctrine, and terrain masking. In Combat Cruise, wingmen are free to maneuver aft between the 100-degree bearing on either side of the flight leader.

items.title: Combat spread checkpoints
items.lede: Combat Spread provides tactical benefit in open terrain and/or if maximum lookout is a primary consideration. Wingmen are free to maneuver from ±10 degrees of the lead aircraft's abeam between 0.5 NM to 2.0 NM maintaining ±100 feet of level in the vertical axis, unless altitude separation is briefed.

items.title: Comm. procedures
items.lede: Communication procedures shall be briefed and may be modified or delegated as required. Aircrews shall minimize radio calls to reduce frequency congestion.

items.title: Communications
items.lede: Communication is the ability to clearly and accurately send and acknowledge information, instructions, or commands, and provide useful feedback. Effective communication is vital to ensuring that all crewmembers understand aircraft and mission status.

items.title: Composite flight plan
items.lede: A composite flight plan is a flight plan which specifies VFR operation for one portion of flight and IFR for another portion. It is used primarily in military operations.

items.lede: A contact approach is one where an aircraft on an IFR flight plan, operating clear of clouds with at least one mile flight visibility and having an ATC authorization, may deviate from the instrument approach procedure and proceed to the airport of destination by visual reference to the ground. Contact approaches initially seem similar to visual approaches, but are subject to much different requirements, and are far more rare.

items.lede: A fundamental principle of flight is attitude plus power equals performance. To obtain desired performance you must maintain the correct attitude and power setting.

items.title: Control pedestal

items.title: Controlling agencies
items.lede: Due to the availability of the Seagull working areas, tactical rigging operations are normally conducted under the control of Seagull RADAR following a normal course rules departure as directed by the squadron's Navigation stage manager.

items.title: Course and timing corrections
items.lede: Both electronic navigation and tactical pilotage can be used during TN missions. A combination of both will optimize course and timing control. Every effort will be made to arrive at the objective on time.

items.title: Course deviations for weather
items.lede: To the extent possible, controllers will issue pertinent information on weather or chaff areas and assist pilots in avoiding such areas when requested. For obvious reasons of safety, an IFR pilot must not deviate from the course or altitude or flight level without a proper ATC clearance.

items.title: CRM callouts
items.lede: CRM improves mission effectiveness by limiting the threat of an error committed by an aircrewmember. Deliberate and expected verbal communication is necessary for error mitigation. Pilots shall be thoroughly familiar with callouts for both pilot flying and pilot monitoring.

items.title: CRM during airdrops
items.lede: During the execution of the Low Level route the PM will handle all normal PM duties as well as conducting all timing and navigation functions.

items.title: CRM during simulated emergencies
items.lede: Emergency checklists are challenge-response-response. Instructors shall ensure the student verbalizes the correct responses to all checklist items.

items.title: CRM inside of objective area (Tilt-Rotor)
items.lede: During the execution of the Low-Level route the PM will handle all normal PM duties as well as conducting all timing and navigation functions.

items.title: CRM seven skills
items.lede: CRM is intended to improve the mission effectiveness of all aviation communities by enhancing crew coordination through increased awareness of associated behavioral skills. Practicing CRM principles will improve mission effectiveness and reduce mishaps that result from poor crew coordination and human error.

items.title: Crosswind takeoff and landing
items.lede: In accomplishing a crosswind takeoff, directional control may be more difficult to maintain. No unusual technique is required in a crosswind landing. Use the wing low method.

items.title: Datum
items.lede: Datum is the position(s) where the search object is expected to be based on its last known position, ground track intentions, and/or known drift factors.

items.title: Ditching - power off
items.lede: The first priority after a dual engine failure is to attempt to regain the use of one or both engines. The altitude and airspeed at the time of the power loss will determine if this is an option.

items.title: Ditching
items.lede: Ditching commenced from low altitudes do not always allow time for more than minimum preparation and planning and may not permit relying on checklists. Therefore, it is essential that each crewmember be thoroughly familiar with ditching procedures and assigned responsibilities.

events.title: Instrument Approaches 2

items.lede: Flight Information Publication (FLIP) documents are used in preflight planning and/or during the flight. Be familiar with the FLIP system and know where to find flight planning information.
terms: FLIP (GP, FIH, and IFR en route supplement, AP (Area Planning) series)

items.title: Dual engine wave-offs
items.lede: Wave-offs allow safe transition from low-powered, descending flight, to high-powered, climbing flight. The maneuver is designed to stop altitude loss as soon as possible while transitioning to a climb at the desired climb speed. Pilots should initiate their own waveoff anytime a safe landing is not possible.

items.title: Due regard
items.lede: Due regard is a phase of flight wherein an aircraft commander of a State-operated aircraft assumes responsibility to separate his/her aircraft from all other aircraft.

items.lede: The dynamic engine cut simulates an engine failure immediately after takeoff with a windmilling prop. It allows practice of critical single-engine skills at a safe altitude. Emphasis is on heading and airspeed control, minimum loss of altitude, and completion of emergency checklist items.

items.title: Electrical system malfunctions
items.lede: Dual-generator failure in a T-44 is a severe emergency requiring prompt decisions in selecting a course of action and reduction of electrical load to limit battery consumption.

items.title: Emergency descent
items.lede: The emergency descent procedure is a maximum effort descent intended to be used for a sustained descent. Aircraft damage and meteorological conditions should be considered. The emergency descent enables maximum altitude loss in minimum time.

items.title: Emergency egress procedures
items.lede: A swing-down door, hinged at the bottom, provides positive cabin security for flight and a stairway for normal and emergency entrance or exit. The emergency exit hatch is located at the third cabin window on the right side.

items.lede: Advise ATC of your minimum fuel status when your fuel supply has reached a state where, upon reaching destination, you cannot accept any undue delay. Be aware this is not an emergency situation, but merely an advisory that indicates an emergency situation is possible should any undue delay occur.
terms: emergency or minimum fuel state and departure procedures

items.lede: A pilot experiencing any emergency during flight shall, as soon as possible after completion of emergency checklists, notify surface craft or ground station in as much detail as possible of the nature of the emergency, assistance desired, pilot intentions, and any other information that might affect safety of flight.
terms: emergency voice reports (souls, fuel, emergency, intentions)

items.lede: En route low altitude charts provide aeronautical information for navigation under IFR conditions below 18,000 feet MSL. En route high altitude charts are designed for navigation at or above 18,000 feet MSL.

items.title: En route timing control techniques
items.lede: Every effort will be made to arrive at the objective on time. All major time adjustments should be completed prior to arrival at the IP.

Section C §16 — Pilot Weather Reports (PIREPs) Format

items.lede: Ensure the weather forecast is updated at least once while en route on all cross-country flights. If weather is deteriorating, it is often better to divert to your alternate early in the flight rather than pressing on with decreasing fuel reserves. Utilize military Pilot to Metro Services (PMSV) or Flight Service Station (FSS) as appropriate.
terms: En route weather facilities (FSS and Metro)

items.title: Engine failure at altitude
items.lede: The T-44 exhibits no unusual handling characteristics at speeds above VMC. Directional control is a function of airspeed and power, varying directly with airspeed and inversely with power.

items.title: Engine failure or fire during or after takeoff

events.title: Cockpit Procedures
events.label: engine failure or fire during or after takeoff

items.lede: If an engine fails during takeoff roll before the aircraft becomes airborne, use the ABORTING TAKEOFF procedure if sufficient runway remains. If an engine failure occurs after takeoff, perform the Engine Failure After Takeoff procedure.
terms: Engine failure or fire during or after takeoff

items.title: Engine fire in flight
items.lede: Fire in flight is a critical emergency requiring the pilot to assess, diagnose, and take prompt corrective action. Illumination of the FIRE warning light is usually the first indication of engine compartment fire.

items.title: Engine fire on deck
items.lede: If an emergency situation dictates immediate discontinuation of engine operation such as fire, fire warning light, brake fire, flameout on deck, etc., request assistance as necessary and execute the Emergency Shutdown On Deck checklist.

items.title: Engine instruments and switches
items.lede: Engine instruments are all located in the left center section of the instrument panel. One three-position toggle switch on the pedestal for each engine will initiate starter motoring and ignition in the IGN & ENG START position or will motor the engine only in the STARTER ONLY position.

items.title: Engine secure and restart
items.lede: In the event engine failure or unexpected flameout occurs, an emergency shutdown should be performed. An airstart may be performed if the engine failure cannot be attributed to a mechanical malfunction or was not accompanied by an explosion, overheating condition, vibration, strong fuel fumes, fire, or zero N1 tachometer rpm.

items.title: Engine start procedures

numbers.label: Operative engine ITT, second engine start
Starter limits
numbers.value: 40 seconds on, 60 seconds off for two cycles; then 40 seconds on, 30 minutes off

items.lede: Engine start is a critical procedure requiring total concentration. Start engines in accordance with NATOPS. Start procedures and actions (up to the After Start Checklist) are performed from memory.

events.label: engine system malfunctions (engine failure or fire after takeoff)

items.lede: An indication of impending engine failure or flameout usually is preceded by unstable engine operation. A flameout condition is indicated by a drop in ITT, torque, and turbine rpm.
terms: engine system malfunctions (engine failure or fire after takeoff)

items.lede: The aircraft is powered by two PT6A-34B turboprop engines rated at 550 shaft horsepower. This engine is a reverse flow, free turbine type, employing a three-stage axial and a single-stage centrifugal compressor assembled as an integral unit.

items.title: Escape
items.lede: After the Green light time has elapsed or the Crewmaster calls "Load clear" the PM will call "Red Light" and begin the escape procedures. The PF will accelerate and clean up while proceeding along the route as covered in the preflight briefing.

items.title: ESIS approach procedures
items.lede: An approach on the Emergency Standby Instrument System is considered a partial panel approach because it does not utilize the primary flight instruments. Failure of the primary flight instruments may occur in various ways including the failure of the primary flight displays (PFD), attitude heading reference systems (AHRS), or electrical failure.

items.title: ESIS operation
items.lede: ESIS provides a visual display of attitude (pitch and roll), and slip/skid information computed from an internal three-axis inertial sensor cluster. The ESIS includes an internal ADC that connects to the aircraft pitot static system and provides baro corrected altitude, air speed, Mach number, and vertical speed information.

items.title: FAA flight plan

numbers.label: File IFR flight plans
numbers.value: at least 30 minutes prior to ETD

items.lede: The information required by the FAA to process flight plans is obtained from FAA Form 7233-4, International Flight Plan. FAA and DoD Flight Plan Forms are equivalent.

items.title: FAA Instrument Flying Handbook
items.lede: This Instrument Flying Handbook is designed for use by instrument flight instructors and pilots preparing for instrument rating tests. Instructors may find this handbook a valuable training aid as it includes basic reference material for knowledge testing and instrument flight training.

items.title: FAA Instrument Procedures Handbook
items.lede: The Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B) is designed as a technical reference for all pilots who operate under instrument flight rules (IFR) in the National Airspace System (NAS). It expands and updates information contained in the FAA-H-8083-15B, Instrument Flying Handbook, and introduces advanced information for IFR operations.

items.lede: In the local area, Corpus approach will normally issue coded climb-out instructions, which can be found in the FAA/CTW-4 LOA in the "In-Flight Guide." For lost communications, make all radio calls "in the blind" and comply with the detailed instructions in FIH or locally in the FAA/CTW-4 LOA.

items.title: Feeder fix selection of IAF
items.lede: A feeder fix is the fix depicted on Instrument Approach Procedure Charts which establishes the starting point of the feeder route. A feeder route is a route depicted on instrument approach procedure charts to designate routes for aircraft to proceed from the en route structure to the initial approach fix (IAF).

numbers.value: 3-5 miles by day, up to 20 miles at night

items.lede: Taxiway lights are blue. Runway edge lights are white, except on instrument runways, where amber replaces white on the last 2000 feet, or half the runway length, whichever is less (to form a caution zone for landings).

items.title: Filing in flight

numbers.label: True airspeed change to report
numbers.value: plus or minus 5 percent, or 10 knots, whichever is greater

items.lede: Simple en route changes to a flight plan, including deviations for weather, can usually be accomplished directly with Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC). If a change in the flight plan is complicated, involves airspace covered by multiple ARTCC facilities, or the ARTCC workload is heavy, the change may have to be filed with FSS.

items.title: Flap malfunctions
items.lede: There are no provisions for emergency flap operation. The aircraft has been flight tested under all possible asymmetric flap configurations and found to be fully controllable within the normal operating envelope.

items.title: Flight control system malfunctions

references.loc: §15.22.3 — Electric Pitch Trim Inoperative or Failed

items.lede: In the event that jamming or binding of flight or engine controls is experienced on the ground, check yaw damper and autopilot OFF, maintain the controls in the jammed or binding condition, and call for immediate inspection.

items.title: Flight control system
items.lede: The aircraft primary flight control system consists of conventional rudder, elevator, and aileron control surfaces. These surfaces are manually operated from the cockpit through mechanical linkage using control wheels for the ailerons and elevators and adjustable rudder/brake pedals for the rudder.

items.title: Flight director malfunctions
items.lede: Flight Director (FD) inputs are received from the onside FGC. When pitch and roll outputs from the individual FGCs are missing or invalid, the red FD flag will appear on the associated PFD.

items.title: Flight instrument characteristics
items.lede: There are six basic flight instruments (attitude indicator, directional indicator, airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI, and turn and slip indicator) which are common to most aircraft. The professional aviator knows not only the functions of these instruments, but their capabilities, limitations, and characteristics.

items.title: Flight integrity
items.lede: Divisions consisting of three aircraft should retain flight integrity to maintain mutual support. Good communication procedures are a prerequisite for maintaining formation integrity.

items.title: Flight schedule
items.lede: The commanding officer or his designated representative is responsible for the promulgation of the flight schedule. The flight schedule is an order of the commanding officer. It shall be followed rigidly and variations require approval of the commanding officer or his designated representative.

items.title: Flight sequence

events.title: Maritime Formation and Aerial Refueling Fundamentals
events.label: flight sequence

items.lede: The formation brief shall be conducted by the Flight Leader and attended by all members of the flight. Only those maneuvers and flight conditions briefed are authorized. The Formation Leader's responsibilities include: conduct the flight in the briefed sequence.

items.title: FMS en route navigation

references.loc: §414 — Flight Management System (FMS) & Global Positioning System (GPS)

items.lede: The FMS is designed to give the pilot centralized control of the navigation sensors and computer based flight planning. The system blends inputs from both VORs, DME, and a GPS to compute present position for display on the CDU.

items.title: FMS management

events.title: Maritime Formation and Aerial Refueling Fundamentals
events.label: FMS management

items.lede: FMS setup for the rendezvous requires the utilization of a discontinuity to display the Seagull boundaries for area orientation while still having the RVIP and RVCP as active waypoints.

items.title: Forced landing
items.lede: If sufficient altitude remains after reaching a suitable landing area, a circular pattern will provide best observation of surface conditions, windspeed and direction. When the condition of the terrain has been noted and the landing area selected, set up a normal pattern and extend the landing gear when the landing is assured.

items.lede: When flying formation, aircraft emergencies or any situation that creates a midair collision threat must be handled quickly and safely. An aircraft with an emergency requiring immediate action will transmit "Knock it off."

items.lede: A formation consists of two or more aircraft flying at minimum safe separation while performing coordinated maneuvers. The Formation Stage reacquaints the student with basic formation flight procedures/principles while introducing formation flight in a multi-engine aircraft with side-by-side seating and limited visibility from the cockpit.
terms: Formation flight procedures and flight sequence

items.title: Formation lead changes
items.lede: During a training flight, lead changes will be made to allow formation members to fly several different positions within the formation. Where lead changes occur is left to the discretion of the mission commander and shall be thoroughly pre briefed.

items.title: Formation radio procedures
items.lede: COMM procedures shall be briefed and may be modified as required. Good COMM procedures are essential for maintaining formation integrity. Aircrews shall minimize radio calls to reduce frequency congestion.

items.title: FSS

references.loc: Section B §1 — FAA Air Traffic Control Procedures
Section C §8 — FAA Pilot-to-Weather Briefer Service

items.lede: Flight Service Stations (FSSs) are air traffic facilities that provide pilot briefings, flight plan processing, en route flight advisories, search and rescue services, and assistance to lost aircraft and aircraft in emergency situations. FSSs also relay ATC clearances, process Notices to Airmen, and broadcast aviation weather and aeronautical information.

events.title: Familiarization Brief
events.label: FTI and NATOPS manual use (verify changes posted)

items.lede: NATOPS Flight Manuals (NFMs) contain flight clearance information, operating procedures and restrictions necessary for flight crews to effectively operate their aircraft. Just as the NATOPS is a guide to the aircraft, the FTI is a guide to the Maritime MPTS curriculum.
terms: FTI and NATOPS manual use (verify changes posted)

items.title: Fuel management panel
items.lede: Cockpit control of the fuel system functions are directed from the fuel management panel. This panel contains the switches for the firewall shutoff valves, boost pumps, fuel transfer pumps, fuel transfer test, a switch for the crossfeed system, fuel system circuit breakers, fuel quantity indicators, and the fuel quantity selector switch.

A crossfeed system permits the use of fuel from all tanks by either engine and is controlled by an electrically actuated valve in the crossfeed line.

items.title: Full-flap landings
items.lede: Full flap landings can dramatically decrease landing roll distance but require higher power settings due to increased drag.

items.title: Full-panel approach-to-stalls
items.lede: Approaches to stalls are practiced in order to recognize an approaching stall and to quickly execute a recovery with minimal altitude loss. Start approaches to stall on assigned altitude and heading at 150 KIAS.

items.title: Full-stop landings

numbers.label: HIGH IDLE, no reverse, maximum braking

items.lede: Dual-engine full-stop landings may be made in any flap configuration. Adjust power to idle at touchdown. Upon ground contact, lower the nosewheel to the runway. Maintain directional control with rudder and apply braking and prop reversing (props full forward) as required by runway length remaining.

items.lede: The only airborne radio equipment required for radar approaches is a functioning radio transmitter and receiver. The radar controller vectors the aircraft to align it with the runway centerline. There are two types of radar approaches: Precision (PAR) and Surveillance (ASR).

items.title: Go/no-go criteria
items.lede: The decision to abort or continue the takeoff is dependent on length of remaining runway, airspeed, gross weight, and density altitude.

items.title: Ground emergencies
items.lede: NATOPS Chapter 13, Ground Emergencies, gives the procedures for an abnormal start, emergency shutdown on deck, loss of brakes, hot brakes and jammed controls on deck.

items.title: Ground procedures
items.lede: Prior to walking to the aircraft, note the BUNO, side number, and location of your Wingman's aircraft on the flight line. This will enable observation of difficulties before and during engine starts.

items.title: Hazardous weather

references.loc: §4.8.4.4 — Hazardous Weather (Icing, Thunderstorms, Turbulence, Volcanic Ash)

items.lede: Thunderstorms, squall lines, and violent turbulence should be regarded as extremely dangerous and must be avoided whenever possible. If it is absolutely necessary to penetrate a thunderstorm, it should be done in the lower third portion of the cell.

items.title: Headset operation
items.lede: Headsets should be utilized by the pilot, copilot, and observer. The electronic noise cancellation system uses an electronically produced signal to cancel the offending noise.

items.title: High altitude approach/penetration

numbers.label: Class C or D, within 4 NM of the primary airport, below 2500 feet AGL

items.lede: The high altitude approach (or penetration) allows the aircraft to maintain an efficient fuel consumption/true airspeed profile and/or to delay descent into low altitude weather (such as an icing layer). High altitude approaches are most common at military fields and are used primarily by fighter type aircraft. ATC will generally assign an alternate procedure for transport category aircraft.

items.title: High-work maneuvers
items.lede: High-work is a general category of any maneuver performed at altitude designed to build basic skills. Emphasis is placed on smooth power manipulation, aircraft control, and trim.

items.lede: Hot brakes usually are caused by excessive or heavy braking action.

items.title: Icing
items.lede: Icing occurs because of supercooled water vapor such as fog, clouds, or rain. The most severe formation will generally occur at an ambient temperature of approximately 23 °F (-5 °C).

items.lede: The transition from instrument to visual flight conditions varies with each approach. Pilots seldom experience a distinct transition from instrument to visual conditions during an approach in obscured weather. The keys to making the transition smooth and precise are preparation and understanding.
terms: IFR landing transition and approach lighting

items.lede: If the aircraft should sustain damage because of a midair collision, bird strike, or overstress, the single most important concern is maintaining or regaining aircraft control. Monitor engine and flight instruments for unusual indications.

items.title: Inadvertent IMC
items.lede: Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC) must be avoided while flying VFR. Occasionally, IMC may be flown into inadvertently even with the best intentions to avoid it.

items.title: Instrument crosscheck
items.lede: The first fundamental skill is cross-checking (also called "scanning" or "instrument coverage"). Cross-checking is the continuous and logical observation of instruments for attitude and performance information.

items.lede: ITO procedures and techniques are used during takeoff at night, over water or deserted areas, and during periods of reduced visibility. Takeoff is accomplished by a combined use of outside visual reference and flight instruments.

items.lede: Aircraft emergencies or any situation that could result in a midair collision must be handled quickly and safely. Any time "KNOCK IT OFF" is called, training is finished, and the formation will return home, as this phrase is used to discontinue the training evolution.

items.title: Landing pattern

numbers.label: Final
numbers.value: 250 feet, 105 KIAS, 1000-1200 feet from the threshold

items.lede: Pattern work is the focus of the Familiarization Stage. The landing pattern consists of upwind, crosswind, downwind, 180 degree position (abeam), approach turn (base), 90 degree position, and final. The landing pattern is a geographic pattern, meaning the aircraft should be flown over the same points each time and adjustments for wind be made with bank angle.

items.lede: Normal landings are descending, decelerating approaches to obtain the optimum angle of attack prior to entering the flare. Adjust power to idle at touchdown. Upon ground contact, lower the nosewheel to the runway. Maintain directional control with rudder and apply braking and prop reversing (props full forward) as required by runway length remaining.

items.title: Landing transition
items.lede: The aircraft is slowed to 120 KIAS, when configuring, and this airspeed is maintained until making the transition to land.

items.title: Lead and Dash-2 responsibilities
items.lede: Roles and responsibilities during formation flight may be fluid and should be pre-briefed. In general, a wingman's role is to gather information and provide it to Lead, and Lead's role is to make the proper decision based on available information.

items.title: Local operations
items.lede: Ground operations involve as many challenges as flight operations. Even though the aircraft is moving far slower than during flight, you are in much closer proximity to hazards such as taxiway lights and other taxiing aircraft.

items.lede: In the event of wheelbrake failure, maintain directional control with rudder, nosewheel steering, or differential power or a combination of all three.

items.lede: The brief should be detailed to the degree that the entire aircrew is aware of the mission profile to include the route, anticipated maneuvers, aircrew currency, and expected altitudes to be flown. A thorough brief is critical to the success of any tactical mission.

items.title: Maintaining aircraft control during emergencies
items.lede: Accuracy is much more important than speed. Maintaining scan and control is imperative during an EP. During any emergency, you should maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation, take the proper action, and land as soon as conditions permit.

items.title: Mechanical stops in throttle quadrant
items.lede: Mechanical stops incorporated in the throttle quadrant prevent rapid forward movement of the power levers from the beta range to the flight range. Downward pressure must be applied to the power levers to permit movement into the flight range and allow power to be added.

items.title: Off-course maneuvering
items.sourcingLead: No publication in the reference set defines or describes off-course maneuvering. The LAT FTI (CNATRA P-912), now in the set, was checked and has no section on it; its only related lines are §108 item 8 ("Do not attempt to re-enter a MTR after leaving the route structure", p. 1-19) and the 45 degree/parallel ridgeline crossing "in cases where your navigation will allow deviation" (§107, p. 1-11). The low-level FTIs have only: do not change heading or airspeed until an exact point of reference is determined, and if the checkpoint has not been identified, turn on time (C-130 Low-Level FTI §105, Tilt-Rotor Low-Level FTI §405); for loss of SA, climb to the MSA (same sections, item 8a); and the optional route width annotation (C-130 §103). Ask the squadron what the item expects before compiling from these.

items.title: On-scene planning – fuel, winds, endurance
items.lede: On scene operations will begin with execution of the Pre-Operations Checklist, followed by the Pre-drop Checklist depending on the situation. The Pre-Operations Checklist includes a briefing on Mission Objectives, operational parameters like airspeed, search altitude, aircraft configuration, etc.

items.title: Operation area
items.lede: High formation flights are usually conducted in established working areas (Juliette, Foxtrot, or Cheetah). At a minimum, a 2000 ft altitude block with VMC conditions is required for the successful completion of the high formation flight.

items.title: Operations below 1000 feet AWL
items.lede: Low altitude, relatively high-speed flight does not leave much room for errors. A plan must be made and briefed prior to descent.

items.title: ORM
items.lede: Operational Risk Management (ORM) is a systematic, decision making process used to identify and manage hazards that endanger naval resources. ORM is a tool used to make informed decisions by providing the best baseline of knowledge and experience available.

items.title: OSC responsibilities

references.loc: Section 1-6 — International SAR System: U.S. Organization

items.lede: The On Scene Commander (OSC) manages the SAR mission on scene as per the Search Action Plan. An OSC has operational authority of the SMC, and operational control of all SRUs on scene.

items.lede: Scanning the sky for other aircraft is a key factor in collision avoidance. It should be used continuously by the pilot and copilot (or right seat passenger) to cover all areas of the sky visible from the cockpit.

items.title: Overhead control panel
items.lede: All aircraft interior lighting is controlled by either rheostat or press-to-light switches located on the overhead control panel. All switches are appropriately placarded as to their identity and function position.

items.title: Overlay approach

references.loc: §414 — Flight Management System (FMS) & Global Positioning System (GPS)

items.lede: The GPS Approach Overlay Program is an authorization for pilots to use GPS avionics under IFR for flying designated non-precision instrument approach procedures, except LOC, LDA, and simplified directional facility (SDF) procedures. These procedures are now identified by the name of the procedure and or "GPS" (e.g., VOR/DME or GPS RWY 15).

items.title: Oxygen system operation and requirements

references.loc: §8.2.4 — Aircraft Oxygen System and Cabin Pressurization

items.lede: The oxygen system is designed primarily as an emergency use system, but may also be used to provide supplemental oxygen at cabin altitudes above 10,000 feet.

items.title: Oxygen system use
items.lede: The oxygen system is designed primarily as an emergency use system, but may also be used to provide supplemental oxygen at cabin altitudes above 10,000 feet.

items.title: P-factor
items.lede: When an aircraft is flying with a high AOA, the "bite" of the downward moving blade is greater than the "bite" of the upward moving blade. This moves the center of thrust to the right of the prop disc area, causing a yawing moment toward the left around the vertical axis.

items.title: PAR versus ASR descent point

numbers.label: PAR approaching glide-path call
numbers.value: approximately 10 to 30 seconds before final descent

items.lede: On an ASR, the controller will inform the pilot of the runway to which the approach will be made, the MDA, and the Missed Approach Point (MAP) location, and will issue advance notice of where the descent to MDA will begin. On a PAR, approximately 10 to 30 seconds before final descent, the controller will advise the aircraft is approaching the glide-path.

items.title: Parade checkpoints
items.lede: Parade is an administrative formation and is used during airfield entry or for a flight demonstration. In general, Parade requires a welded wing formation with each wingman using power to maintain a briefed bearing and separation.

items.title: Pattern considerations
items.lede: Pattern work is the focus of the Familiarization Stage. Pattern work will teach you to safely recover the aircraft in both normal and emergency situations.

items.title: Performance data

numbers.label: One-engine-inoperative climb gradient
numbers.value: 200 feet per nautical mile, or the published gradient

items.lede: The NATOPS performance chapters present performance data necessary for preflight and in-flight mission planning and include explanatory text on the use of the charts. The charts are designed to enable the pilot to determine the capability of the T-44C aircraft for takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, glide, and landing.

items.title: Personal and emergency equipment
items.lede: The T-44C survival equipment outfitting, cockpit configuration, and mission capabilities are unique to training class aircraft. The emphasis is placed on aircraft mounted (contractor supported) equipment rather than man mounted survival equipment.

items.title: PIC CRM during SSE
items.lede: The pilot in command is responsible for safety of flight and, in this regard, must determine that emergency procedures are properly completed. He may delegate accomplishment of certain phases of the emergency procedures to other crewmembers.

items.title: PIC CRM
items.lede: Pilot in command refers to the pilot of an individual aircraft. The pilot in command is responsible for the safe, orderly flight of the aircraft and well-being of the crew.

items.title: PIC decision making
items.lede: Decision Making is the ability to choose a course of action using logical and sound judgment based on available information. The pilot in command is responsible for the safe, orderly flight of the aircraft and well-being of the crew.

items.title: Pilot-controlled lighting

numbers.label: Lights stay on
numbers.value: 15 minutes from the most recent activation

references.loc: Section B §7 — Pilot Control of Airport Lighting

items.lede: Radio control of lighting is available at selected airports to provide airborne control of lights by keying the aircraft's microphone. Control of lighting systems is often available at locations without specified hours for lighting and where there is no control tower or FSS or when the tower or FSS is closed (locations with a part-time tower or FSS) or specified hours.

items.title: Pilot instrument panel
items.lede: The EFIS is made up of a pilot side and copilot side system. Each side is functionally and physically isolated from each other, and is capable of functioning as a complete, independent system.

items.title: Pilot monitoring duties during airdrops
items.lede: During the execution of the Low Level route the PM will handle all normal PM duties as well as conducting all timing and navigation functions.

items.title: Pilot monitoring responsibilities
items.lede: The pilot that is not manipulating the controls of the aircraft is considered the pilot monitoring. The pilot monitoring can be in either seat and may switch throughout the flight.

items.title: Pilot monitoring and right seat responsibilities
items.lede: The copilot shall assist the pilot in command in the safe and successful accomplishment of the assigned flight and is considered the second in command of the aircraft. The crewmember in the right seat normally assumes the copilot duties.
terms: Pilot monitoring and right seat responsibilities

items.title: Pitot-static system
items.lede: The pitot and static air system provides two separate sources of static and ram air. The system consists of two pitot masts mounted on either side of the aircraft nose, four static air pressure ports, two in the aircraft exterior skin on each side of the aft fuselage, and the associated plumbing.

items.title: Point-to-point navigation
items.lede: Bearing and range information from a VOR/DME or TACAN facility is sufficient for navigating direct to any point within reception range.

items.title: Porpoised landings
items.lede: A porpoised landing may occur if the nose-wheel touches down before the main-mounts.

items.lede: Good communication procedures are a prerequisite for maintaining formation integrity and can be divided as internal and external communications. Internal communications involve only Lead and Wing. External communications are between the flight and ATC, other aircraft, etc.

items.title: Right seat positioning
items.lede: One of the differences between the left and right seat is the relative position of the power levers. You will control the aircraft with your right hand on the yoke and your left hand on the power levers.

items.lede: OPNAVINST 3710.7 establishes the Naval Air Training and Operating Procedures Standardization (NATOPS) program. The NATOPS program is a positive approach towards improving combat readiness and achieving a substantial reduction in aircraft mishaps.

items.title: Scatter plan
items.sourcingLead: No publication in the reference set defines or describes a scatter plan. The LAT FTI (CNATRA P-912) was checked and does not mention one (its KIO list in §108, p. 1-19, includes "Two or more aircraft lose sight", which is not a scatter plan). The term appears only as a brief line item: C-130 Low-Level FTI Appendix A §A100 (NATOPS Brief), Formation Brief item 11.e "Scatter / rejoin plan" (p. A-7). Related text: C-130 Low-Level FTI §201 (rejoin points by distance-to-go and MSL altitude); Tilt-Rotor Low-Level FTI §203 (lost sight, IIMC fan break) and §309 (airborne rendezvous and holding). items.title: Search ideology and phraseology
items.lede: The ultimate goal of search planning is to find the survivors of a distress incident as quickly as possible. The way to achieve this goal is to increase the cumulative Probability of Success (POS) as quickly as possible using available and assigned resources.

items.title: Search patterns

numbers.label: Sector search radius, aircraft
numbers.value: generally not greater than 20 to 30 miles

items.lede: A coded system is used to designate search patterns. The major pattern characteristic is designated by the first letter. The second letter denotes either a single (S) or multiple (M) unit search. The third letter designates specialized SRU instructions.

items.title: Seat and rudder pedal adjustment
items.lede: The cockpit seats are adjustable fore and aft with the inboard handle on each pilot seat and vertically with the outboard handle. A two-position fore and aft adjustment of the pedals is provided through control levers on each pedal.

items.lede: The proper steps for securing the aircraft must be based on the time the aircraft will be left unattended, the aircraft weight, the expected wind direction and velocity, and the anticipated availability of ground and aircrews for mooring and/or evacuation.

items.title: See and avoid

references.loc: §4-4-15 — Use of Visual Clearing Procedures and Scanning Techniques

items.lede: When meteorological conditions permit, regardless of type of flight plan or whether or not under control of a radar facility, the pilot is responsible to see and avoid other traffic, terrain, or obstacles. You must never forget you are responsible for looking outside and scanning for traffic.

items.title: Sequence of events
items.lede: Only those maneuvers and flight conditions briefed are authorized. Adjustments can be made in flight but shall be briefed prior to execution.

items.lede: A simulated dual engine failure allows practice of restart procedures and may be followed by a simulated ditch. Simulated ditches shall not be practiced with an engine actually secured or a prop feathered.

items.title: Simulated emergency scenarios
items.lede: Simulated emergency training is necessary to develop fully qualified flightcrews. The simulated emergencies must be reasonable, applicable, and must not create a condition hazardous to flight safety not normally encountered in an actual emergency.

items.title: Simulated versus actual EP
items.lede: Simulated emergency training is conducted during all phases of instruction. Practicing emergencies is required to develop fully qualified and confident flight crews. All emergencies shall be conducted in accordance with NATOPS and the FTI.

items.title: Slow down
items.lede: Slowdown occurs at a pre briefed point. Slowdown should be accomplished early enough to allow all aircraft to be stabilized at drop altitude (1000' AGL) and airspeed (130 KIAS) 1 minute prior to green light.

items.lede: Attempt to locate, isolate, and extinguish the fire or source of smoke or fumes prior to initiating the smoke removal procedures. If the source of smoke/fumes cannot be readily determined and eliminated, proceed with the Smoke/Fire of Unknown Origin Checklist.

items.lede: The purpose of the VT-35 SOP is to provide VT-35 pilots with standardized procedures to be followed during flight operations. Prior to each brief, students shall ensure they have access either via tablet or navigation bag to all updated and current required publications, including the VT-31 and VT-35 Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) and the TW-4 SOP.

items.lede: The SSE landing pattern acquaints the student with procedures required to land safely following the loss of an engine. The SSE pattern is very similar to a normal pattern except considerations are made for decreased performance and reduced directional control.

items.lede: STARs and Flight Management System Procedures (FMSP) [used only by aircraft with FMS] are arrival routes established to simplify clearance delivery procedures and facilitate transition between en route and instrument approach procedures. Expect to fly a STAR if one exists for the destination.

items.title: Survivor relocation pattern
items.lede: The Survivor Relocation Pattern (SRP) is a maneuver flown to relocate a surface target after the crew has lost sight of it.

items.title: Tactical formation mission brief
items.lede: A thorough brief is critical to the success of any tactical mission. Tactical briefing guide located in Appendix A and NATOPS blue card shall be utilized.

items.title: Takeoff
items.lede: After power is stabilized above 70-percent N1, smoothly apply maximum allowable power. Monitor ITT and torque. At rotation, set takeoff attitude by raising the nose 7 to 10° noseup pitch.

items.lede: TAS is an airborne system used for detecting and tracking aircraft near your own aircraft. The TAS processor and antennas detect and track other aircraft by interrogating their transponders. Should the TAS processor determine that a possible collision hazard exists, it issues visual and aural advisories to the crew.

items.lede: The primary purpose of TERPS (FAA Order 8260.3) is to provide safe terminal procedures for aircraft operating to and from military and civil airports. The main considerations include criteria for obstacle clearance, descent/climb gradients, and landing minimums.

items.title: The six Ts

TEM is the execution tool for CRM and is the link between operational risk management and the seven critical skills of CRM.

items.title: Turbulence
items.lede: Even though flight in severe turbulence is to be avoided, turbulent air may be encountered under certain conditions. During night or instrument flight conditions, it is not always possible to find in-between areas of low turbulence or calm conditions. When areas of expected turbulence must be penetrated, be ready to counter rapid changes in attitude and to accept major indicated altitude variations.

items.lede: Ground minimum control speed (VMC GRD) is the minimum speed at which the aircraft can maintain runway centerline using rudder/aileron inputs alone (no brakes/loss of nosewheel steering) if an engine fails during the takeoff run.

items.title: Wake turbulence

numbers.label: Interval after a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go

items.lede: Every aircraft generates wake turbulence while in flight. Wake turbulence is a function of an aircraft producing lift, resulting in the formation of two counter-rotating vortices trailing behind the aircraft.

items.title: Weather considerations during emergencies
items.lede: In the event of a loss of usable power the pilot in command shall land as soon as possible. Consideration should be given to landing at the nearest suitable airport, when time, weather conditions, terrain, facilities, and resources available indicate that a safe landing can be accomplished.

items.title: Weather filing criteria

items.lede: A DD-175-1 Flight Weather Briefing Form, or "Dash One," shall be completed whenever an IFR flight plan is filed. Comply with directives (CNAF, SOPs) for takeoff, filing, and weather avoidance criteria.

items.lede: The pilot in command should ensure proper loading of the aircraft before each flight. The three elements of proper aircraft loadings are weight, balance, and restraint.

items.title: Wet compass characteristics

references.loc: Ch. 5 — The Basic Aviation Magnetic Compass

items.lede: The magnetic compass located on the top of the windshield divider may be used in the event of compass system failure or for instrument crosscheck. Reading should be taken only during level unaccelerated flight.

items.title: Wind shear

numbers.label: Windshear
numbers.value: airspeed change of 10 knots or more and/or vertical speed change greater than 500 fpm

items.lede: A windshear is defined as any rapid change in wind direction and/or speed that results in an airspeed change of 10 knots or more and/or a vertical speed change greater than 500 fpm. Windshear at low altitudes is a potential hazard to the T-44C during takeoff, landing, and all low-altitude operations.

items.title: Windshield heating
items.lede: Windshield heat for both the pilot and copilot windshields is controlled by a toggle switch on the pilot subpanel placarded WSHLD ANTI-ICE BOTH, OFF, and PILOT. A controller with a temperature sensing unit maintains 95 °F temperature at the windshield surface.

items.title: Wing or uncontrollable fire
items.lede: Fire in flight is a critical emergency requiring the pilot to assess, diagnose, and take prompt corrective action. There is little that can be done to control a wing fire except to shut off fuel and electrical systems that may be contributing to the fire or which could aggravate it.

items.title: WW versus convective SIGMET
items.lede: There are four types of inflight aviation weather advisories: the SIGMET, the Convective SIGMET, the AIRMET, and the Center Weather Advisory (CWA). The Severe Weather Watch Bulletins (WWs), (with associated Alert Messages) (AWW) supplements these Inflight Aviation Weather Advisories.
